title: Death close
hook: sixty days facing the end, to live better now

segments.voice: Yesterday, five doors in one hallway. Your line was they differ. Did anyone tell you what their door says? Today, the last day of facing the end, and the first step back outside. Day eight hundred eighteen.

This block has run sixty days. It opened with the oldest question, and a page where you wrote what you think. Since then: Socrates weighing sleep against a journey, the Buddha's last words, a boy waiting at Death's door, a mourner's prayer that never mentions death, Martha and the resurrection, an atom's weight of good, Zhuangzi's skull, marigolds and lanterns, hospice nurses, tea, a letter for after. Today the block closes, and it closes on the point the whole thing was for.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS.` →`THE OLDEST QUESTION.` → `WHAT IT WAS FOR.`

segments.voice: First, number our days, the psalm this block already sat with once. It asks, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." The counting isn't there to frighten. It's there to make a heart wise, now. Second, the woods. Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond, and he said why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." Death is in the sentence, but the sentence is about living. Third, back to the day. Marcus, in his notebook, wrote of passing each day as if it were the last, neither frantic nor numb, so the day in front of him would be done well. Different homes, one direction of travel: the end looked at squarely, and then the face turned back toward today. Fourth, live, then. That is the line this block ends on. It isn't a promise about what happens after. The traditions differ on that, and we left them differing. It's what these teachers did once they had looked at death: they went back into the day, a little more awake.
screen: `NUMBER OUR DAYS.` · `THE WOODS.` · `BACK TO THE DAY.` · `LIVE, THEN.` · then, large: `DEATH CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Go outside, if you can. A step, a balcony or an open window is enough. Stand or sit where the air moves. Breathe in, and notice that it's this air, today's air. Breathe out, and let the sixty days be finished. There's nothing to conclude. If you like, say the line silently on each out-breath: live, then. Let your eyes find one thing out there that is alive, a tree, a bird, a person walking past, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Death close. The end of sixty days facing death, closed the way these teachers closed it: by turning back toward the day. Today's word.
Your line: live, then. Today, do one ordinary thing deliberately, as Thoreau put it: a meal, a walk, a conversation, done awake. Tomorrow a new block begins, on love. Day eight hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: People on many paths keep death in view as a way of living more fully: Psalm 90 is read in Jewish and Christian worship, Stoics wrote notes to themselves about the end, and some readers return to Thoreau's Walden for its call to live deliberately.
